tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

format.description: Export format. Only csv is supported.

limit.description: Maximum number of flow records to return. Default 100.

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

startTime.description: Start of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Overrides timeRange when set.

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

  - Ports unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080
  - This routes across all pods with app=recommendation-engine, giving ~50/50 since there are 2 stable + 2 canary replicas

- Pods running:

  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Running
- Service now targets both versions via shared label

- Traffic split is approximated by pod count. Adjust replicas on engine-v2-1 vs engine-v2-0 to shift the ratio.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint to run /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing a CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Updated the pod spec to start nginx in the foreground:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]

Current state
- Deployment app (crashloop-test) is healthy.
- New ReplicaSet: app-784bb86f68
- Pod app-784bb86f68-b52qg: 1/1 Ready, Running, 0 restarts.
- Deployment status: Available=True, ReadyReplicas=1.

Want me to also add readiness/liveness probes or revert the command override and use the image defaults instead?

results.taskOutput:
I fixed the deployment.

What was wrong
- The Pod was failing with ImagePullBackOff:
  - Initial image was quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag (tag doesn’t exist).
  - Changing to quay.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable still failed with 401 UNAUTHORIZED from the registry.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a public, pullable image:
  - image: docker.io/library/nginx:stable-alpine

Current status
- Deployment app is Available (minimum availability met).
- 1 replica Ready.
- Running Pod: app-54cd45f8c-gcs6k (1/1 Running).

Let me know if you prefer a different nginx image (e.g., an unprivileged variant) or if you want me to:
- Configure an imagePullSecret for quay.io and switch back.
- Increase replicas above 1.
- Pin to a specific version tag.

I fixed the deployment.

What was wrong
- The Pod was failing with ImagePullBackOff:
  - Initial image was quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag (tag doesn’t exist).
  - Changing to quay.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable still failed with 401 UNAUTHORIZED from the registry.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a public, pullable image:
  - image: docker.io/library/nginx:stable-alpine

- Deployment app is Available (minimum availability met).
- 1 replica Ready.
- Running Pod: app-54cd45f8c-gcs6k (1/1 Running).

- Configure an imagePullSecret for quay.io and switch back.

- Pin to a specific version tag.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed the deployment.

What was wrong
- The Pod was failing with ImagePullBackOff:
  - Initial image was quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag (tag doesn’t exist).
  - Changing to quay.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable still failed with 401 UNAUTHORIZED from the registry.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a public, pullable image:
  - image: docker.io/library/nginx:stable-alpine

Current status
- Deployment app is Available (minimum availability met).
- 1 replica Ready.
- Running Pod: app-54cd45f8c-gcs6k (1/1 Running).

Let me know if you prefer a different nginx image (e.g., an unprivileged variant) or if you want me to:
- Configure an imagePullSecret for quay.io and switch back.
- Increase replicas above 1.
- Pin to a specific version tag.

Pod is stable. Verification successful.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". With no bound volume, the scheduler couldn’t place the pod.

What I changed
- Removed the unbound PVC and recreated it using the cluster’s default StorageClass "standard" (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce). No data was lost since the PVC was never bound.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi on standard)
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns): Running and Ready (container started successfully)

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust.

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Fixed.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". With no bound volume, the scheduler couldn’t place the pod.

What I changed
- Removed the unbound PVC and recreated it using the cluster’s default StorageClass "standard" (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce). No data was lost since the PVC was never bound.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi on standard)
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns): Running and Ready (container started successfully)

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". With no bound volume, the scheduler couldn’t place the pod.

What I changed
- Removed the unbound PVC and recreated it using the cluster’s default StorageClass "standard" (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce). No data was lost since the PVC was never bound.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi on standard)
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns): Running and Ready (container started successfully)

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment used:
  - Liveness/readiness probes on port 80 with paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist)
  - Service targetPort 80
- This caused connection refused on probes and the pod to be killed repeatedly.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to:
  - Port: 8080
  - Path: /
- Exposed container port 8080 (the manifest now lists 80 and 8080; the Service targets 8080, which is what matters).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80 for in-cluster access).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7d8467cb84-z7kkk — 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service: ClusterIP orders/webapp on port 80 -> 8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ from a pod in the cluster

Optional next steps
- If you want external access, I can create an Ingress/Route.
- If you prefer specific health endpoints, tell me the paths and I’ll update probes.
- Need to scale? Say the replica count you want.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  replicas: 1
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: http
          protocol: TCP
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        resources: {}
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment used:
  - Liveness/readiness probes on port 80 with paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist)
  - Service targetPort 80
- This caused connection refused on probes and the pod to be killed repeatedly.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to:
  - Port: 8080
  - Path: /
- Exposed container port 8080 (the manifest now lists 80 and 8080; the Service targets 8080, which is what matters).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80 for in-cluster access).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7d8467cb84-z7kkk — 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service: ClusterIP orders/webapp on port 80 -> 8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ from a pod in the cluster

Optional next steps
- If you want external access, I can create an Ingress/Route.
- If you prefer specific health endpoints, tell me the paths and I’ll update probes.
- Need to scale? Say the replica count you want.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  replicas: 1
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: http
          protocol: TCP
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        resources: {}
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  selector:
    app: webapp
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  replicas: 1
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: http
          protocol: TCP
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        resources: {}
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  selector:
    app: webapp
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment used:
  - Liveness/readiness probes on port 80 with paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist)
  - Service targetPort 80
- This caused connection refused on probes and the pod to be killed repeatedly.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to:
  - Port: 8080
  - Path: /
- Exposed container port 8080 (the manifest now lists 80 and 8080; the Service targets 8080, which is what matters).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80 for in-cluster access).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7d8467cb84-z7kkk — 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service: ClusterIP orders/webapp on port 80 -> 8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ from a pod in the cluster

Optional next steps
- If you want external access, I can create an Ingress/Route.
- If you prefer specific health endpoints, tell me the paths and I’ll update probes.
- Need to scale? Say the replica count you want.

results.taskOutput:
Cause
- The Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role didn’t grant any permissions on core API pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so the pod-reader service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Left the existing RoleBinding (pod-reader-binding) as-is; it already binds the pod-reader ServiceAccount to this Role in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

Result
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note
- This grants access only within simple-rbac-setup. If you need pod read access across namespaces, create a ClusterRole with these rules and bind it with a RoleBinding per namespace (or a ClusterRoleBinding if appropriate).

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Cause
- The Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role didn’t grant any permissions on core API pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so the pod-reader service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Left the existing RoleBinding (pod-reader-binding) as-is; it already binds the pod-reader ServiceAccount to this Role in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

Result
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note
- This grants access only within simple-rbac-setup. If you need pod read access across namespaces, create a ClusterRole with these rules and bind it with a RoleBinding per namespace (or a ClusterRoleBinding if appropriate).

outputSteps.content:
Cause
- The Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role didn’t grant any permissions on core API pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so the pod-reader service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Left the existing RoleBinding (pod-reader-binding) as-is; it already binds the pod-reader ServiceAccount to this Role in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

Result
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note
- This grants access only within simple-rbac-setup. If you need pod read access across namespaces, create a ClusterRole with these rules and bind it with a RoleBinding per namespace (or a ClusterRoleBinding if appropriate).

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Mismatch in selector: The Service nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints and could not route traffic.
- Wrong targetPort: The container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, while the Service targeted port 80. Result: even once endpoints exist, traffic to port 80 on the Pod wasn’t accepted.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods:
  - spec.selector: app=nginx
- Corrected the port mapping:
  - spec.ports[0]: port: 80, targetPort: 8080, name: http

Current state (verified)
- Service: ClusterIP 10.97.97.248:80 -> Pod:8080
- Endpoints now point to the running Pod:
  - 10.244.0.27:8080
- In-cluster access works:
  - From the nginx Pod: curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned 200
  - ClusterIP http://10.97.97.248 returned 200

How you can verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sI http://nginx

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Switch the Service to NodePort:
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
- Or create a LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it):
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
- Or use an Ingress/Route in front of the Service.

Tell me how you want it exposed (NodePort, LoadBalancer, or Ingress), and I can configure it.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Mismatch in selector: The Service nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints and could not route traffic.
- Wrong targetPort: The container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, while the Service targeted port 80. Result: even once endpoints exist, traffic to port 80 on the Pod wasn’t accepted.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods:
  - spec.selector: app=nginx
- Corrected the port mapping:
  - spec.ports[0]: port: 80, targetPort: 8080, name: http

Current state (verified)
- Service: ClusterIP 10.97.97.248:80 -> Pod:8080
- Endpoints now point to the running Pod:
  - 10.244.0.27:8080
- In-cluster access works:
  - From the nginx Pod: curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned 200
  - ClusterIP http://10.97.97.248 returned 200

How you can verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sI http://nginx

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Switch the Service to NodePort:
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
- Or create a LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it):
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
- Or use an Ingress/Route in front of the Service.

Tell me how you want it exposed (NodePort, LoadBalancer, or Ingress), and I can configure it.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Mismatch in selector: The Service nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints and could not route traffic.
- Wrong targetPort: The container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, while the Service targeted port 80. Result: even once endpoints exist, traffic to port 80 on the Pod wasn’t accepted.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods:
  - spec.selector: app=nginx
- Corrected the port mapping:
  - spec.ports[0]: port: 80, targetPort: 8080, name: http

Current state (verified)
- Service: ClusterIP 10.97.97.248:80 -> Pod:8080
- Endpoints now point to the running Pod:
  - 10.244.0.27:8080
- In-cluster access works:
  - From the nginx Pod: curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned 200
  - ClusterIP http://10.97.97.248 returned 200

How you can verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sI http://nginx

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Switch the Service to NodePort:
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
- Or create a LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it):
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
- Or use an Ingress/Route in front of the Service.

Tell me how you want it exposed (NodePort, LoadBalancer, or Ingress), and I can configure it.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu), but your only node has no such label. Scheduler couldn’t place the pods (FailedScheduling), leaving the Service with no endpoints — hence connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending with “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints.
  - The node mcp-eval-cluster has no label environment=production-gpu.

Fix applied
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods are Running:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-lpx2b (10.244.0.30)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-wtxsv (10.244.0.31)
  - Service endpoints now populated:
    - 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80

Why this resolves the error
- With pods now running and registered as endpoints, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will be forwarded to the backing pods instead of being refused.

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to restrict these pods to GPU nodes, add the matching label to the node first, then reintroduce the selector:
  - Label the node: kubectl label node mcp-eval-cluster environment=production-gpu
  - Add the selector back to the Deployment spec.template.spec.nodeSelector.
- Optional hardening: add liveness/readiness probes so endpoints are only added when the container is ready.

Want me to add readiness/liveness probes or restore a selector after labeling the node?

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu), but your only node has no such label. Scheduler couldn’t place the pods (FailedScheduling), leaving the Service with no endpoints — hence connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending with “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints.
  - The node mcp-eval-cluster has no label environment=production-gpu.

Fix applied
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods are Running:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-lpx2b (10.244.0.30)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-wtxsv (10.244.0.31)
  - Service endpoints now populated:
    - 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80

Why this resolves the error
- With pods now running and registered as endpoints, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will be forwarded to the backing pods instead of being refused.

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to restrict these pods to GPU nodes, add the matching label to the node first, then reintroduce the selector:
  - Label the node: kubectl label node mcp-eval-cluster environment=production-gpu
  - Add the selector back to the Deployment spec.template.spec.nodeSelector.
- Optional hardening: add liveness/readiness probes so endpoints are only added when the container is ready.

Want me to add readiness/liveness probes or restore a selector after labeling the node?

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu), but your only node has no such label. Scheduler couldn’t place the pods (FailedScheduling), leaving the Service with no endpoints — hence connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending with “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints.
  - The node mcp-eval-cluster has no label environment=production-gpu.

Fix applied
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods are Running:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-lpx2b (10.244.0.30)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-wtxsv (10.244.0.31)
  - Service endpoints now populated:
    - 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80

Why this resolves the error
- With pods now running and registered as endpoints, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will be forwarded to the backing pods instead of being refused.

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to restrict these pods to GPU nodes, add the matching label to the node first, then reintroduce the selector:
  - Label the node: kubectl label node mcp-eval-cluster environment=production-gpu
  - Add the selector back to the Deployment spec.template.spec.nodeSelector.
- Optional hardening: add liveness/readiness probes so endpoints are only added when the container is ready.

results.taskOutput:
Below is a complete, multi-document YAML you can kubectl apply to set up the requested multi-tenant environment. It creates the namespaces, service accounts, RBAC (full access in each dev namespace; read-only to dev-shared; no grants for staging/prod), resource quotas, and network policies (default-deny everywhere except system namespaces; devs can reach their own namespace and dev-shared; staging/prod isolated; DNS allowed).

Apply with:
kubectl apply -f dev-multitenant.yml

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-alice
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-bob
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-charlie
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: charlie
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-shared
  labels:
    env: dev
    shared: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: prod
  labels:
    env: prod

# ServiceAccounts per developer
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie

# Roles: full control in each dev namespace (exclude RBAC APIs to avoid privilege escalation)
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-alice
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-bob
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-charlie
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get"]

# Bind users and their SAs to their own namespace Role
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: owner-binding
  namespace: dev-alice
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: alice-sa
    namespace: dev-alice
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: namespace-owner
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: owner-binding
  namespace: dev-bob
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: bob
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: bob-sa
    namespace: dev-bob
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: namespace-owner
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: owner-binding
  namespace: dev-charlie
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: charlie
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: charlie-sa
    namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: namespace-owner

# Read-only Role in dev-shared and bindings for dev users and their SAs
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: readonly
  namespace: dev-shared
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: readonly-developers
  namespace: dev-shared
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
  - kind: User
    name: bob
  - kind: User
    name: charlie
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: alice-sa
    namespace: dev-alice
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: bob-sa
    namespace: dev-bob
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: charlie-sa
    namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: readonly

# ResourceQuotas
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-standard
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-standard
  namespace: dev-bob
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-standard
  namespace: dev-charlie
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-shared
  namespace: dev-shared
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 8Gi
    pods: "20"
    services: "10"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-staging
  namespace: staging
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "20"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-prod
  namespace: prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "20"

# NetworkPolicies
# Helper: Default deny (Ingress+Egress) for all non-system namespaces
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]

outputSteps.content:
Below is a complete, multi-document YAML you can kubectl apply to set up the requested multi-tenant environment. It creates the namespaces, service accounts, RBAC (full access in each dev namespace; read-only to dev-shared; no grants for staging/prod), resource quotas, and network policies (default-deny everywhere except system namespaces; devs can reach their own namespace and dev-shared; staging/prod isolated; DNS allowed).

Apply with:
kubectl apply -f dev-multitenant.yml

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-alice
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-bob
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-charlie
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: charlie
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-shared
  labels:
    env: dev
    shared: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: prod
  labels:
    env: prod

# ServiceAccounts per developer
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie

# Roles: full control in each dev namespace (exclude RBAC APIs to avoid privilege escalation)
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-alice
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-bob
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-charlie
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get"]

# Bind users and their SAs to their own namespace Role
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: owner-binding
  namespace: dev-alice
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: alice-sa
    namespace: dev-alice
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: namespace-owner
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: owner-binding
  namespace: dev-bob
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: bob
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: bob-sa
    namespace: dev-bob
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: namespace-owner
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: owner-binding
  namespace: dev-charlie
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: charlie
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: charlie-sa
    namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: namespace-owner

# Read-only Role in dev-shared and bindings for dev users and their SAs
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: readonly
  namespace: dev-shared
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch", "autoscaling", "extensions", "networking.k8s.io", "policy"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: readonly-developers
  namespace: dev-shared
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
  - kind: User
    name: bob
  - kind: User
    name: charlie
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: alice-sa
    namespace: dev-alice
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: bob-sa
    namespace: dev-bob
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: charlie-sa
    namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: readonly

# ResourceQuotas
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-standard
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-standard
  namespace: dev-bob
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1

    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-shared
  namespace: dev-shared
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 8Gi
    pods: "20"
    services: "10"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-staging
  namespace: staging
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "20"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-prod
  namespace: prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "20"

# NetworkPolicies
# Helper: Default deny (Ingress+Egress) for all non-system namespaces
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: dev-bob
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: dev-charlie
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: dev-shared
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

  namespace: staging
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]

# Allow same-namespace traffic for dev namespaces (needed after default deny)
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-same-namespace
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: {}
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector: {}
---

  podSelector: {}

# Allow dev namespaces to reach dev-shared only (blocks cross-developer comms)
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: allow-egress-to-dev-shared
